summary: A request from the University of Illinois for other network users interested in IBM's MPSX mixed integer programming package on the UCLA CCN 360/91. CCN did not yet have it, and it carried a fixed monthly rental. Illinois hoped to share the cost among several users. The estimate given was $130 a month plus $225 for the mixed integer feature.

eli5.summary: A group wants to buy a special tool that costs money each month. They ask if anyone else wants to use it so everyone can share the bill.

questions: mpsx mixed integer programming on the network
sharing the cost of software on the arpanet
subtitle: Seeking network sites to share the cost of an optimization software package.

tldr.problem: The University of Illinois wants to use IBM's MPSX mixed integer programming software at the UCLA CCN facility, but the monthly rental fee is too high for one site to bear.
tldr.mechanism: The university asks other ARPANET sites if they want to share the cost. A monthly lease is $130 plus $225 for the mixed integer feature, and costs would be prorated among all users.
tldr.outcome: The RFC seeks network partners to collectively purchase access to MPSX and share the operating expense.

today: RFC 345 is a May 1972 request to share software costs on the early ARPANET. It is marked Unknown status. This is an example of how ARPANET users experimented with collaborative resource sharing in the earliest days of network computing.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
RFC 345 is a request from Karl Kelley at the University of Illinois for other ARPANET sites interested in a special software package. The software is MPSX (IBM's mathematical programming system for optimization), a newer version that outperforms the older MPS package.

MPSX is an IBM product and carries a fixed monthly rental fee. The University of Illinois would like to install MPSX at the UCLA CCN (Compleat Computer Network), which runs a shared 360/91 available to ARPANET users, but only if the costs can be split among several sites.
sections.eli5: A school wants to rent special math software on a shared computer network. Instead of one school paying for it, they ask all the schools that want to use it to split the bill.

sections.title: The Offer
sections.content:
The estimated cost is $130 per month for the base MPSX system, plus $225 for the mixed integer programming feature. Each site using the system would be charged a prorated share of this cost. CCN would handle billing details and account setup for participating sites.

The RFC names Stewart Schuster at the University of Illinois as the contact for questions about the mixed integer programming feature itself. Meanwhile, the basic MPS system is already available on the CCN computer, so sites can experiment with it while the decision is being made.
sections.eli5: The monthly fee is $130 plus $225, split among all users. Each site pays their share. The school's contact person can answer technical questions, and you can already try the older version.

sections.title: Call for Interest
sections.content: Karl Kelley asks interested sites to contact him within the month. This RFC is essentially a survey to determine if there is enough interest to justify the installation and cost-sharing arrangement. Participating sites would benefit from access to a powerful optimization tool shared across the ARPANET without each site bearing the full expense.
sections.eli5: If your site wants to use it, email the person listed to say yes. He needs to know soon so he can set it up.
